claim: Functional diversity of midbrain dopamine (DA) neurons ranges across multiple scales, from differences in intrinsic properties and connectivity to selective task engagement in behaving animals.
source: Functional diversity of midbrain dopamine (DA) neurons ranges across multiple scales, from differences in intrinsic properties and connectivity to selective task engagement in behaving animals.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature establishing this diversity across multiple biological scales.

claim: Distinct in vitro biophysical features of DA neurons have been associated with different axonal projection targets.
source: Distinct in vitro biophysical features of DA neurons have been associated with different axonal projection targets.
evidence: This claim references established findings from prior in vitro studies.

claim: Differences in burst firing exist among DA neurons projecting to dorsolateral striatum.
source: We identified differences in burst firing among DA neurons projecting to dorsolateral striatum.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Bursting differentiated DA neurons in the medial substantia nigra (SN) projecting either to dorsal or ventral striatum.
source: Bursting also differentiated DA neurons in the medial substantia nigra (SN) projecting either to dorsal or ventral striatum.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data comparing different projection-defined populations.

claim: Differences in mean firing rates exist among ventral tegmental area (VTA) DA neurons projecting to lateral or medial shell of nucleus accumbens.
source: We found differences in mean firing rates and pause durations among ventral tegmental area (VTA) DA neurons projecting to lateral or medial shell of nucleus accumbens.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data comparing VTA DA neuron populations.

claim: Differences in pause durations exist among ventral tegmental area (VTA) DA neurons projecting to lateral or medial shell of nucleus accumbens.
source: We found differences in mean firing rates and pause durations among ventral tegmental area (VTA) DA neurons projecting to lateral or medial shell of nucleus accumbens.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: The midbrain dopamine system has emerged as a parallel processor carrying out multiple functions rather than a single global computation.
source: Rather than a single global computation, the midbrain DA system has therefore emerged as a parallel processor carrying out multiple functions (Haber, 2014; Kegeles et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Projection-identified groups of DA neurons have marked differences in intrinsic biophysical properties and input-output relationships.
source: This showed that projection-identified groups of DA neurons, including those that project to specific subregions of the striatum, have marked differences in intrinsic biophysical properties and input-output relationships (Lammel et al., 2008; Tarfa et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior in vitro studies.

claim: Individual DA axons show extensive arborisation often across distinct striatal territories.
source: However, this idea is somewhat challenged by virally-mediated single DA neuron labelling studies that depicted the extensive arborisation of individual axons often across distinct striatal territories (Aransay et al., 2015; Matsuda et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior viral tracing studies.

claim: A ventrolateral SN DA population is most severely affected in Parkinson disease.
source: In PD, a ventrolateral SN DA population is most severely affected (Damier et al., 1999; Fu et al., 2016; Gibb and Lees, 1991; Kordower et al., 2013), which might be indicative for an innate and/or acquired differential vulnerability towards alpha-synuclein aggregation-mediated neurodegeneration (Surmeier et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior clinical and pathological studies.

claim: In schizophrenia, PET-studies in patients strongly suggested an early and selective dysregulation of a DA subpopulation projecting to associative, dorsomedial striatal regions.
source: In schizophrenia, PET-studies in patients strongly suggested an early and selective dysregulation of a DA subpopulation projecting to associative, dorsomedial striatal regions (Kegeles et al., 2010; McCutcheon et al., 2019), but cellular substrates have remained elusive.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to PET imaging studies in schizophrenia patients.

claim: A hierarchical sequence of DA release in different striatal territories has been identified in models of drug addiction.
source: In models of drug addiction, a hierarchical sequence of DA release in different striatal territories has been identified (Willuhn et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on drug addiction models.

claim: Selective hyperactivity in mesolimbic-projecting DA subpopulations has been identified as a causal factor in depression-like behaviors in depression models based on chronic social defeat.
source: In depression models, based on chronic social defeat, selective hyperactivity in mesolimbic-projecting DA subpopulations has been identified as a causal factor in depression-like behaviors using projection-selective optogenetic interventions (Cao et al., 2010; Chaudhury et al., 2013; Tye et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior optogenetic studies in depression models.

claim: Application of conventional retrograde tracing protocol (2% fluorogold; 500 nl; 50 nl/min) in the dorsal striatum resulted in structural damage of nigrostriatal axons one week after infusion.
source: We noticed that the application of a conventional retrograde tracing protocol (2% fluorogold (FG); 500 nl; 50 nl/min; Liu et al., 2003) in the dorsal striatum (DS; bregma: 0.86 mm, lateral: 2.0 mm, ventral: 2.8 mm) resulted in structural damage of nigrostriatal axons already one week after infusion (Figure 1A, column one, FG-0, note reduced TH expression).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and imaging data showing reduced TH expression.

claim: No apparent structural damage was observed using a ten-fold FG-dilution (0.2%).
source: In contrast, we observed no apparent structural damage using a ten-fold FG-dilution (0.2%, Figure 1A, FG-1, 2nd column from left), but surprisingly failed to detect any stable in vivo spontaneously active DA neurons in the substantia nigra (SN), again one week after infusion (N = 3;~10 tracts per animal, intra-nigral speed of electrode advancement 60 µm/min; coverage 4–5 mm Z-depth from skull, data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and imaging data.

claim: 0.2% FG infusion resulted in failure to detect any stable in vivo spontaneously active DA neurons in the substantia nigra one week after infusion.
source: In contrast, we observed no apparent structural damage using a ten-fold FG-dilution (0.2%, Figure 1A, FG-1, 2nd column from left), but surprisingly failed to detect any stable in vivo spontaneously active DA neurons in the substantia nigra (SN), again one week after infusion (N = 3;~10 tracts per animal, intra-nigral speed of electrode advancement 60 µm/min; coverage 4–5 mm Z-depth from skull, data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental recording data.

claim: 0.002% FG constitutes the lowest detectable concentration for retrograde labeling.
source: With this strategy, we identified 0.002% FG (FG-3) to be the lowest concentration where a significant proportion (ca. 20–30%) of SN DA neurons displayed detectable tracer levels based on intrinsic FG fluorescence (Figure 1A, FG-3, column four; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, signal to noise 3:1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the dilution series and imaging analysis.

claim: Approximately 20-30% of SN DA neurons displayed detectable tracer levels at 0.002% FG concentration based on intrinsic FG fluorescence.
source: With this strategy, we identified 0.002% FG (FG-3) to be the lowest concentration where a significant proportion (ca. 20–30%) of SN DA neurons displayed detectable tracer levels based on intrinsic FG fluorescence (Figure 1A, FG-3, column four; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, signal to noise 3:1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data.

claim: The rate of detection of FG-labeled neurons was improved by using a FG-antibody combined with a fluorescently-labelled secondary antibody.
source: This rate of detection was further improved by using a FG-antibody (see Materials and methods) combined with a fluorescently-labelled secondary antibody (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental comparison of detection methods.

claim: FG-immunoreactivity within DA neurons showed selective immunostaining in cytoplasmic vesicles, most likely to be lysosomes.
source: Detailed inspection of the cellular distribution of FG-immunoreactivity within DA neurons revealed selective immunostaining in cytoplasmic vesicles, most likely to be lysosomes (Wessendorf, 1991).
evidence: This claim is based on microscopic observations and supported by citation to prior work on FG localization.

claim: Retrograde tracing with 1000-fold diluted FG (0.002%) did not perturb any in vivo electrophysiological property of DA lSN neurons.
source: In summary, retrograde tracing with 1000-fold diluted FG did not perturb any in vivo electrophysiological property of DA lSN neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by comprehensive comparison of electrophysiological parameters between control and FG-labeled neurons showing no significant differences.

claim: There were no significant differences in firing frequency between control DA lSN neurons and FG-3-labelled DA lSN neurons (control: 3.51 ± 0.41 Hz, FG: 3.51 ± 0.4 Hz).
source: In line with the examples shown in Figure 2, quantitative analysis of firing frequency (means ± SEMs; control: 3.51 ± 0.41 Hz, FG: 3.51 ± 0.4 Hz; panel 3B), regularity (CV; control: 62.92 ± 7.55%, FG: 58.84 ± 7.29%; panel 3B) and quantitative descriptors of ISI-distribution patterns (kurtosis (control: 4.1 ± 0.73, FG: 3.69 ± 0.69), skewness (control: 0.98 ± 0.18, FG: 0.88 ± 0.16) and a firing pattern categorization based on a theoretical model called GLO (see Materials and methods), panel 3B) did not reveal any significant differences between the two populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The overall topographic patterns of cellular distributions of retrogradely traced DA neurons was in accordance with those from previous work using retrobeads or retrograde viral tracers.
source: The overall topographic patterns of cellular distributions (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1) was in accordance with those from previous work using retrobeads (Lammel et al., 2008) or retrograde viral tracers (Lerner et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of current anatomical mapping data with cited prior studies.

claim: The medial SN is a region where DA cell bodies of three distinct, equally prevalent axonal projections intermingle (approximately 30% DLS, 40% DMS, 30% lNAcc).
source: Our data revealed a high complexity within the medial SN, where DA cell bodies of three distinct, equally prevalent axonal projections intermingled (mSN;~30% DLS,~40% DMS,~30% lNAcc).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of retrograde tracing data.

claim: In the lSN, approximately 70% of DA neurons project to DLS.
source: By contrast, in the two neighboring regions, the lSN and the lateral VTA (parabrachial pigmented nucleus (PBP), paranigral nucleus (PN)), only one axonal projection was dominant (~70% DLS-projecting DA neurons in the lSN;~60% lNAcc in the PBP,~70% mNAcc in the PN).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of retrograde tracing data.

claim: In the PBP, approximately 60% of DA neurons project to lNAcc.
source: By contrast, in the two neighboring regions, the lSN and the lateral VTA (parabrachial pigmented nucleus (PBP), paranigral nucleus (PN)), only one axonal projection was dominant (~70% DLS-projecting DA neurons in the lSN;~60% lNAcc in the PBP,~70% mNAcc in the PN).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of retrograde tracing data.

claim: In the PN, approximately 70% of DA neurons project to mNAcc.
source: By contrast, in the two neighboring regions, the lSN and the lateral VTA (parabrachial pigmented nucleus (PBP), paranigral nucleus (PN)), only one axonal projection was dominant (~70% DLS-projecting DA neurons in the lSN;~60% lNAcc in the PBP,~70% mNAcc in the PN).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of retrograde tracing data.

claim: Only the dorsolateral striatum receives two equally prominent axonal projections from the mSN and the lSN, in contrast to dorsomedial and ventral striatum.
source: Indeed, only the dorsolateral striatum, in contrast to dorsomedial and ventral striatum, received two equally prominent axonal projections from the mSN and the lSN (Figure 4F2).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical tracing data showing dual sources for DLS projections.

claim: Double-labelling retrograde tracing experiments found only a small percentage (4-14%) of double-labelled DA neurons.
source: In accordance to our previous study (Lammel et al., 2008), we found only a small percentage, varying between 4–14%, of double-labelled DA neurons (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of double-tracing experiments.

claim: Small variations in isoflurane concentrations in the range between 1-2% did not correlate with differences in firing frequencies or patterns in any of the studied DA projections.
source: This approach was very stable across animals (>70% of animals, the isoflurane concentration was 1.2% in 100% O2, flow rate 350 ml/min) and the small variations in isoflurane concentrations in the range between 1–2% did not correlate with differences in firing frequencies or patterns in any of the studied DA projections (see Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of anesthesia depth and neuronal activity.

claim: During anesthesia under the stated conditions, oscillatory cortical activity observed under lighter isoflurane anesthesia was largely suppressed.
source: Moreover, during anesthesia, under the conditions stated above, oscillatory cortical activity, observed under lighter isoflurane anesthesia, was largely suppressed (see see Figure 4—figure supplement 4G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by LFP recordings at different anesthesia depths.

claim: Firing frequencies and patterns of mSN/VTA DA neurons under anesthesia were comparable to those in corresponding DA neurons recorded previously in freely moving, awake mice in the homecage.
source: In addition, we found that firing frequencies and patterns of mSN/VTA were comparable to those in corresponding DA neurons recorded previously in freely moving, awake mice in the homecage (for detailed comparison, see Figure 4—figure supplement 4D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with previously published data from awake recordings.

claim: About 40% of DLS-projecting DA neurons in the lSN (6 of 15) displayed robust bursting (SFB >5%) throughout the recording period.
source: Importantly, while about 40% of DLS-projecting DA neurons in the lSN (n = 6 of 15) displayed this type of robust bursting (SFB >5%) throughout the recording period, none of the identified DLS-projecting DA neurons located in the mSN (n = 0 of 9) fired in this bursty manner (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of burst firing in recorded neurons.

claim: None of the identified DLS-projecting DA neurons located in the mSN (0 of 9) displayed robust bursting (SFB >5%).
source: Importantly, while about 40% of DLS-projecting DA neurons in the lSN (n = 6 of 15) displayed this type of robust bursting (SFB >5%) throughout the recording period, none of the identified DLS-projecting DA neurons located in the mSN (n = 0 of 9) fired in this bursty manner (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of burst firing showing complete absence in mSN.

claim: Using the variables burstiness (SFB), relative AP trough and precision of spiking (log(σ2)), DLS-projecting SN DA neurons could be accurately classified into lateral and medial groups with a predictive power of 79.2% (p<0.05).
source: Using the variables burstiness (SFB), relative AP trough and precision of spiking (log(σ2)), we could accurately classify the remaining DLS-projecting SN DA neurons into a lateral and medial group with a predictive power of 79.2% (p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by linear discriminant analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: When using the entire data set to train the linear classifier, almost all (92.6%) of DLS-projecting SN DA neurons were classified correctly into lateral and medial groups.
source: When using the entire data set to train the linear classifier, almost all (92.6%) of DLS-projecting SN DA neurons were classified correctly (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by linear discriminant analysis results.

claim: No differences were found between any parameters of mSN DA populations projecting to DLS versus DMS.
source: Here, we found no differences between any parameters of these two mSN DA populations projecting to different territories of the dorsal striatum (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of electrophysiological parameters.

claim: Linear discriminant analysis based on the best set of parameters did not perform above chance (50.9%) in discriminating DLS- from DMS-projecting DA neurons in the medial SN.
source: Accordingly, the linear discriminant analysis (LDA) based on the best set of parameters (CV, SFB, skewness of the ISI-distribution, pauses per minute, the mean oscillation period (GLO) and the relative AP trough) did not perform above chance (50.9%) in discriminating DLS- from DMS-projecting DA neurons in the medial SN.
evidence: This claim is supported by linear discriminant analysis showing no discrimination ability.

claim: Most electrophysiological parameters describing the patterns of discharge including bursts and pauses, as well as the shapes of the ISI-distributions (Kurtosis, Skewness) were significantly different between dorsal (n = 18) and ventral (n = 14) striatum projecting mSN DA neurons.
source: Apart from mean frequencies and AP waveforms, which were similar, most electrophysiological parameters describing the patterns of discharge including bursts (Figure 7D) but also pauses (Figure 7E), as well as the shapes of the ISI-distributions (Kurtosis, Skewness; Figure 7F) were significantly different between dorsal (n = 18) and ventral (n = 14) striatum projecting mSN DA neurons (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of multiple electrophysiological parameters.

claim: Linear discriminant analysis based on skewness of the ISI-distribution, AP duration, relative AP trough and the precision of spiking (log(σ2)) showed a strong trend to classify mSN DA neurons into dorsal or ventral striatum projecting cells with a predictive power of 70.8% (p<0.07).
source: The linear discriminant analysis (LDA) based on the best set of parameters (skewness of the ISI-distribution, AP duration, relative AP trough and the precision of spiking (log(σ2)) showed a strong trend to classify mSN DA neurons into dorsal or ventral striatum projecting cells with a predictive power of 70.8%, when using half of the data set for training (p<0.07).
evidence: This claim is supported by linear discriminant analysis results.

claim: When the entire data set was used for LDA, 84.4% of mSN DA neurons were classified correctly into dorsal or ventral striatum projecting groups.
source: When the entire data set was used, 84.4% of mSN DA neurons were classified correctly (Figure 7G).
evidence: This claim is supported by linear discriminant analysis results.

claim: No significant differences were found between lateral shell NAcc-projecting DA neurons localized in the mSN compared to those positioned in the VTA.
source: Furthermore, a functional comparison of lateral shell NAcc-projecting (TARGET) DA neurons localized in the mSN compared to those positioned in the VTA (SOURCES), the classical location of mesolimbic DA neurons, revealed no significant differences (see Figure 7—figure supplement 3) between the groups, violating the VTA/SN anatomical boundary.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of electrophysiological parameters between mSN and VTA neurons with the same projection target.

claim: VTA DA neurons projecting to lateral shell of nucleus accumbens have higher mean firing rates than those projecting to medial shell.
source: We next asked whether distinct ventral striatal-projecting populations (i.e. lateral shell NAcc vs medial shell NAcc-projecting neurons) also show functional differences in vivo, given that these two populations displayed very distinct electrophysiological properties in vitro (Lammel et al., 2008). Figure 8 compares the electrophysiological properties of two DA neurons in the VTA, projecting either to lateral shell (lNAcc) or medial shell (mNAcc) of nucleus accumbens. The 10 s recording traces, 30 s raster plots and the two ISI histograms display selective differences in mean discharge frequency and the duration of pauses only (Figure 8A and B), which are also evident at the population level (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing firing rates between the two populations.

claim: VTA DA neurons projecting to medial shell of nucleus accumbens have longer pause durations than those projecting to lateral shell.
source: The 10 s recording traces, 30 s raster plots and the two ISI histograms display selective differences in mean discharge frequency and the duration of pauses only (Figure 8A and B), which are also evident at the population level (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing pause durations between the two populations.

claim: All other functional in vivo properties did not differ between lNAcc- and mNAcc-projecting VTA DA neurons.
source: In contrast, all other functional in vivo properties – including analyzed AP waveform parameters - did not differ between the two populations (see Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison showing no differences in other parameters.

claim: The in vivo results showing higher firing rates in lateral shell NAcc-projecting DA neurons compared to medial shell NAcc DA neurons are surprising in light of previous in vitro data.
source: In light of the previous in vitro data, where medial shell NAcc-projecting DA neurons showed higher firing rates compared to lateral shell NAcc DA neurons, our in vivo results are surprising.
evidence: This claim represents an interpretation comparing current in vivo findings with prior in vitro studies.

claim: The longer in vivo pauses observed in medial shell NAcc projecting VTA DA neurons are in line with their very long in vitro post-inhibition rebound delays.
source: In contrast, the longer in vivo pauses observed in medial shell NAcc projecting VTA DA neurons are in line with their very long in vitro post-inhibition rebound delays.
evidence: This claim represents an interpretation connecting in vivo pause data with prior in vitro findings.

claim: None of the subsets of variables used for linear discriminant analysis showed a segregation of lNAcc- and mNAcc-projecting mesolimbic DA populations above chance level.
source: Note that none of the subsets of variables used for linear discriminant analysis showed a segregation of these two mesolimbic DA populations above chance level.
evidence: This claim is supported by linear discriminant analysis results.

claim: The success rate of identifying and labelling spontaneously active mPFC-projecting DA neurons was not sufficient (ca. 10%) to carry out a systematic study.
source: While we succeeded in labelling and anatomically mapping this sparse DA subpopulation with our FG-3-protocol, the success rate of identifying and labelling spontaneously active mPFC-projecting DA neurons was not sufficient (ca. 10%) to carry out a systematic study (Figure 8—figure supplement 2; 1 of 10 recorded and labelled VTA neurons was identified to be dopaminergic and projecting to mPFC).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental recording data showing low success rate.

claim: All n = 102 DA neurons in this study were labelled and immunohistochemically identified, thus avoiding the uncertainties of 'putative' DA populations.
source: Importantly, all n = 102 DA neurons in this study were labelled and immunohistochemically identified, thus avoiding the uncertainties of 'putative' DA populations.
evidence: This claim describes a methodological feature of the study supported by the experimental protocol.

claim: The study controlled for functional perturbations by retrograde labelling itself, based on the high-dilution fluorogold protocol.
source: Moreover, our study controlled for functional perturbations by retrograde labelling itself, based on our high-dilution fluorogold protocol.
evidence: This claim describes a methodological feature validated by comparison with control neurons.

claim: The large degree of functional diversity regarding burst firing among SN DA neurons projecting to dorsolateral striatum was not anticipated.
source: We did not anticipate the large degree of functional diversity regarding burst firing among those SN DA neurons projecting to dorsolateral striatum.
evidence: This represents an interpretation of the unexpected nature of the findings.

claim: In vivo bursting of DA neurons in the medial SN was exclusively associated with cells projecting to lateral shell of nucleus accumbens.
source: Furthermore, we were surprised to find in vivo bursting of DA neurons in the medial SN to be exclusively associated with cells projecting to lateral shell of nucleus accumbens.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing bursting only in lNAcc-projecting mSN neurons.

claim: The difference in mean firing rates between slower-discharging DA neurons projecting to medial shell and faster-firing DA neurons projecting to lateral shell of nucleus accumbens was unexpected given their respective intrinsic excitabilities.
source: Finally, the difference in mean firing rates between slower-discharging DA neurons projecting to medial shell and faster-firing DA neurons projecting to lateral shell of nucleus accumbens was unexpected given their respective intrinsic excitabilities.
evidence: This represents an interpretation comparing in vivo findings with prior in vitro data on intrinsic excitability.

claim: All in vivo electrophysiological data were recorded under isoflurane anesthesia.
source: Importantly, all in vivo electrophysiological data were recorded under isoflurane anesthesia.
evidence: This describes a methodological constraint of the study.

claim: The study cannot directly draw conclusions about behaviorally relevant activity patterns in DA subpopulations but rather identifies differences in in vivo baseline excitability.
source: Therefore, we cannot directly draw conclusions about behaviorally relevant activity patterns in DA subpopulations but rather identify differences in in vivo baseline excitability.
evidence: This represents an acknowledgment of the study's limitations due to anesthesia.

claim: Differences in in vivo firing rates between VTA DA neurons identified under isoflurane anesthesia in a mouse model of cognitive impairment were recapitulated in awake behaving animals.
source: In addition, we also showed that differences in in vivo firing rates between VTA DA neurons identified under isoflurane anesthesia in a mouse model of cognitive impairment (Krabbe et al., 2015), were recapitulated in awake behaving animals (Duvarci et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies comparing anesthetized and awake recordings.

claim: Task-related differences in firing were only revealed in awake behaving animals.
source: However, the task-related differences in firing were only revealed in awake behaving animals (Duvarci et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work in awake animals.

claim: The mesocortical DA subpopulation might either be particularly vulnerable to the labelling protocol or mostly silent under isoflurane anesthesia.
source: The unique mismatch between the extent of retrograde labelling and the difficulty of identifying and recording mesocortical DA neurons in vivo indicated that this DA subpopulation might either be particularly vulnerable to our labelling protocol or mostly silent under isoflurane anesthesia.
evidence: This represents speculation about the reasons for low recording success of mPFC-projecting neurons.

claim: Mesocortical DA neurons being mostly silent under isoflurane anesthesia is not unlikely given the evidence for orexinergic modulation of mesocortical DA neurons.
source: The latter possibility is not unlikely given the evidence for orexinergic modulation of mesocortical DA neurons (Del Cid-Pellitero and Garzón, 2014).
evidence: This speculation is supported by citation to prior work on orexinergic modulation.

claim: The study focused on rostral striatal areas not covering the caudal 'tail' region, which is a projection area of DA neurons located in the SN pars lateralis.
source: Furthermore, our study focused on rostral striatal areas not covering the caudal 'tail' region, which is a projection area of DA neurons located in the SN pars lateralis.
evidence: This describes a limitation in the anatomical coverage of the study.

claim: The DA projection to the caudal 'tail' region has been shown to be involved in the computing of aversive stimuli and stable visual memories in rodents and non-human primates.
source: This DA projection has been shown to be involved in the computing of aversive stimuli and stable visual memories in rodents and non-human primates (Kim et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2015a; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009; Menegas et al., 2018; Menegas et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior functional studies.

claim: It is crucial to control whether labelling itself will change functional properties of targeted neurons in vivo.
source: Given that labelling of DA subpopulations – for identification and/or optogenetic manipulation – has become an essential tool, we believe it is crucial to control whether the labelling itself will change functional properties of the targeted neurons in vivo.
evidence: This represents a methodological recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: Virally-mediated GFP-expression in SN DA neurons leads to robust changes in their intrinsic firing pattern.
source: In addition to the effect of conventional concentrations of fluorogold, we have previously shown that virally-mediated GFP-expression in SN DA neurons leads to robust changes in their intrinsic firing pattern (Schiemann et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work from the authors' lab.

claim: The findings are in line with a previous study that found differences in in vitro excitability, including T-type calcium channel mediated rebound excitability, between calbindin-positive and calbindin-negative SN DA neurons.
source: While the underlying mechanisms need to be resolved, our findings are in line with a previous study from the Khaliq lab that found differences in in vitro excitability, including T-type calcium channel mediated rebound excitability, between calbindin-positive and calbindin-negative SN DA neurons (Evans et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim connects current findings with prior in vitro work through citation.

claim: DLS-projecting SN DA neurons have larger HCN-currents compared to DMS-projecting SN DA neurons, which might enhance rebound excitability and possibly in vivo bursting.
source: Also, Lerner and colleagues demonstrated larger HCN-currents in DLS-projecting SN DA neurons compared to DMS-projecting SN DA neurons, which might further enhance rebound excitability and possibly in vivo bursting (Lerner et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and includes speculation about functional implications.

claim: Different degrees of activity-dependent calcium loading might play a crucial role for selective neurodegeneration in Parkinson disease.
source: An influential hypothesis regarding the differential vulnerability between distinct DA subpopulations in Parkinson disease proposes that different degrees of activity-dependent calcium loading might play a crucial role for selective neurodegeneration (Surmeier et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a hypothesis in the literature.

claim: The high in vivo burstiness of lateral SN DA neurons might be an attractive new target for protective intervention in Parkinson disease.
source: Given that the lateral SN is the most vulnerable DA region in PD (Damier et al., 1999; Gibb and Lees, 1991), we believe that the high in vivo burstiness of lateral SN DA neurons might be an attractive new target for protective intervention.
evidence: This represents speculation about therapeutic implications based on the study's findings and prior knowledge.

claim: K-ATP channel dependent burst mechanisms might be operative in lateral shell-projecting rather than dorsal striatum-projecting DA neurons in the medial SN.
source: This implies that K-ATP channel dependent burst mechanisms, which we previously identified to be selective for the medial SN (Schiemann et al., 2012), might be operative in lateral shell-projecting rather than dorsal striatum-projecting DA neurons in this region.
evidence: This represents inference based on current findings and prior work on burst mechanisms.

claim: Selective dysregulation in DA projections to dorsomedial striatum has been associated with schizophrenia.
source: The mechanism for this region-specific absence of bursting are currently unknown but might be highly relevant given that selective dysregulation in DA projections to dorsomedial striatum has been associated with schizophrenia (Kegeles et al., 2010; McCutcheon et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: DA neurons become phase-locked to prefrontal 4 Hz rhythms during working memory tasks, which might result in rhythmic bursting.
source: However, we and others have recently shown that DA neurons become phase-locked to prefrontal 4 Hz rhythms during working memory tasks, which might also result in rhythmic bursting (Duvarci et al., 2018; Fujisawa and Buzsáki, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies on DA neuron activity during behavior.

claim: Mesolimbic DA neurons projecting to medial versus lateral shell of accumbens constitute two parallel pathways.
source: Finally, our study gives further support to the idea that mesolimbic DA neurons projecting to medial versus lateral shell of accumbens constitute two parallel pathways.
evidence: This represents an interpretation of the study's findings in the context of DA system organization.

claim: Recent studies highlighted the differential functional roles of medial versus lateral shell NAcc DA projections, as well as their distinct circuit affiliations.
source: Recent studies highlighted the differential functional roles of these DA projections, as well as their distinct circuit affiliations (de Jong et al., 2019; Lammel et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent functional studies.

claim: The firing frequency data suggest that medial and lateral shell projecting DA neurons operate at different baseline excitation/inhibition (E/I) setpoints in vivo.
source: Our firing frequency data suggest that these two DA projections operate at different baseline excitation/inhibition (E/I) setpoints in vivo.
evidence: This represents an interpretation of the firing rate differences observed in the study.

claim: Medial shell projecting DA neurons, which displayed high intrinsic excitability in vitro, discharged in vivo at a lower rate, which might be indicative for a higher degree of tonic net inhibition.
source: In particular, medial shell projecting DA neurons, which displayed high intrinsic excitability associated with sustained high frequency firing in vitro (Lammel et al., 2008), discharged in vivo at a lower rate, which might be indicative for a higher degree of tonic net inhibition.
evidence: This represents an interpretation connecting in vivo and in vitro findings with speculation about network inhibition.

claim: >95% of retrogradely FG-3-labelled neurons in both the SN and the VTA were TH-positive (dopaminergic).
